Lessons.Title: Tiling the Plane
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Compare how much region is covered by different shapes in a tiling, and justify area-preserving rearrangements.

A tiling covers the plane without gaps or overlap. Different shapes can have different area even when each is counted as one tile. In an original model, take one small triangular tile as 1 area unit; a matching rhombus is worth 2 such units and a matching trapezoid is worth 3.

In the public source's patterned hexagon grouping, 3 red trapezoids, 4 blue rhombi and 7 green triangles contribute 9, 8 and 7 small-triangle area units per hexagon. Across eight such groups, the red, blue and green contributions are 72, 64 and 56 triangular area units. Comparing by tile count alone misleads: the source asks students to justify which shape family covers more in two differently arranged eight-hexagon patterns. This numerical decomposition supplements, but does not replace, student comparison of actual patterns or discussion of several defensible 'which one does not belong' arguments.

KeyConcepts.Title: Tiling without gaps
KeyConcepts.Definition: A tiling completely covers a target region using shapes without gaps or overlap.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A visible blank space means the proposed design does not tile the entire target region.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two neighboring triangular pieces may meet edge to edge; a white gap means their union leaves some region uncovered.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compare unlike tiles
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different polygons may cover different amounts of the plane.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Convert each tile into a shared area unit, then multiply by tile count.
KeyConcepts.Example: With small triangle area 1, a rhombus has area 2 and a trapezoid has area 3 triangular units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Conservation by rearrangement
KeyConcepts.Definition: Moving or rotating unchanged shapes preserves their total combined area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Require pieces to neither overlap nor leave the intended combined region incomplete.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two trapezoids have the same area as three rhombi or six smaller triangles under the shared unit model: 6 units.

WorkedExamples.Title: Which shapes cover the greatest area?
WorkedExamples.Question: In a new tiled design, there are 3 red trapezoids, 4 blue rhombi and 7 green small triangles. One rhombus has the area of 2 triangles; one trapezoid has the area of 3. Which color contributes most area?
WorkedExamples.Method: Change every polygon type into the same small-triangle area unit, then compare totals.
Steps: Red: 3 trapezoids × 3 triangular units each = 9.
Blue: 4 rhombi × 2 triangular units each = 8.
Green: 7 triangles × 1 unit each = 7.
Compare 9 > 8 > 7 to conclude red covers the largest total area.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The red trapezoids cover 9 triangular area units, more than blue's 8 or green's 7.
WorkedExamples.Check: The fewest tiles can cover the greatest area when individual tile shapes are larger.

WorkedExamples.Title: Make three equal-area mosaics
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare an arrangement of 2 trapezoids, an arrangement of 3 rhombi and an arrangement of 6 small triangles. Can they cover equal area without gaps or overlap?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use a common area unit and describe valid complete arrangements.
Steps: Two trapezoids contribute 2 × 3 = 6 triangular area units.
Three rhombi contribute 3 × 2 = 6 triangular area units.
Six small triangles contribute 6 × 1 = 6 triangular area units.
All arrangements cover 6 units, provided they form non-overlapping complete regions.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Yes; each design covers 6 small-triangle area units despite different polygon counts.
WorkedExamples.Check: A student-created drawing must demonstrate that the pieces meet without gaps or overlap; this is a teacher-reviewed claim.

WorkedExamples.Title: Explain a tiling comparison
WorkedExamples.Question: Make two differently shaped patterns using the same set of movable pieces. Give two mathematically justified reasons why the patterns can look different while covering the same total area.
WorkedExamples.Method: Open-ended visual justification for teacher review.
Steps: Identify the area contributed by each unchanged piece.
Construct a second complete, non-overlapping arrangement.
Explain what changed in the outline and what did not change about the pieces.
Present more than one defensible visual comparison or classification.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The outlines and color arrangements may differ while the total area is unchanged because every piece is used exactly once.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher rubric checks unit choice, complete coverage, equal piece inventory and explanation quality; it is not automatically graded from one number.

WorkedExamples.Title: Eight hexagons: count covered area rather than colored tiles
WorkedExamples.Question: In a first-party eight-hexagon schematic of the source task, each hexagon contains 3 red trapezoids, 4 blue rhombi and 7 green triangles. Each trapezoid has the same area as 3 small triangles and each rhombus as 2. Across all eight hexagons, which color occupies the greatest total area? Explain whether rearranging these unchanged tiles into another complete eight-hexagon pattern changes their area.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare one hexagon using small-triangle units, scale the composition to eight matching hexagons and justify conservation under rearrangement.
Steps: One hexagon contains 3 × 3 = 9 red, 4 × 2 = 8 blue and 7 × 1 = 7 green small-triangle area units.
Eight such hexagons contain 24 trapezoids, 32 rhombi and 56 triangles.
Convert tile counts to comparable area: red = 24 × 3 = 72, blue = 32 × 2 = 64 and green = 56 × 1 = 56 small-triangle units.
Compare 72 > 64 > 56: red covers the greatest area, even though green has more individual tiles.
Rearrange without stretching, gaps, overlaps or missing pieces: the pattern outline may change, but the total colored area stays 72 + 64 + 56 = 192 triangular area units.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Red covers the greatest amount of the plane: 72 triangular area units, compared with blue 64 and green 56. A rearrangement using all unchanged tiles preserves each color's area.
WorkedExamples.Check: The 3/4/7 ratio describes each constituent hexagon, not the entire eight-hexagon image. This original numerical schematic does not recreate or verify the historical publisher images, move/rotate applet or an actual student drawing; those require separate source figure and teacher-rubric evidence.

WorkedExamples.Title: Four original pattern descriptions: more than one defensible classification
WorkedExamples.Question: Consider four text-only pattern scenarios for the same target region: A is covered by one blue polygon type without gaps, B by one yellow polygon type without gaps, C by both blue and yellow polygon types without gaps, and D by both types with uncovered white spaces. Give a reason that D differs from the other three, then offer a different mathematically defensible grouping.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use stated coverage, number of tile types and color composition as independent comparison criteria; do not infer unknown lengths or areas.
Steps: A, B and C explicitly cover the target without gaps; D has an uncovered region and therefore does not completely tile that target.
A and B are single-shape-type descriptions, while C and D each involve two shape types.
A and C contain blue tiles, whereas B does not; a classification by color is valid if identified as color-based rather than area-based.
Explain why a gap makes D different when the criterion is complete tiling, but color or tile variety can lead to different legitimate categories.
WorkedExamples.Answer: D is the only pattern described as leaving part of its target uncovered. Alternatively, A and B use only one tile type while C and D use two. A chosen justification must identify the actual criterion.
WorkedExamples.Check: These are accessible text-only first-party scenarios modeled on public source task categories, not checked reproductions of the four historical pictures. Multiple classifications and explanations require teacher review.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming seven little triangles cover more area than three trapezoids because seven is a larger count.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Counts are incomparable until the areas of individual unlike polygons use one common unit.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Break larger tiles into small-triangle units before adding their colored areas.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling any colorful pattern a complete tiling.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Blank uncovered regions or overlapping pieces violate coverage of the intended region.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check all boundaries and explain whether a whole region is covered without gaps or overlap.

SummaryPoints: A true tiling covers its target without gaps or overlaps.
Use a common area unit to compare different polygon shapes, not just tile counts.
Multiple arrangements can differ visually while preserving the same total covered area.

Visuals.Title: Equivalent small-triangle areas of three polygon types
Visuals.Description: First-party text-accessible equivalent-area tile-family schematic, NOT the source image: a small green triangle is one triangular area unit; a blue rhombus composes 2 of these triangles and a red trapezoid 3. One component hexagon contains 7 green triangles (area 7), 4 blue rhombi (area 8), and 3 red trapezoids (area 9). For an eight-hexagon construction with this same inventory in every hexagon, green occupies 56, blue 64 and red 72 triangular units. These are triangular area units, NOT square units. A and B in the historical source may differ in arrangement; the authored textual visual does not reproduce publisher images or assert a working interactive applet.
SecondaryItems: Eight source-style hexagon groups: red 72, blue 64, green 56 triangular area units

Visuals.Title: Accessible first-party tiling comparison (not original figure recreation)
Visuals.Description: Four verbally specified target-region designs: A consists only of blue polygonal tiles and has no gaps or overlaps; B consists only of yellow tiles and has no gaps or overlaps; C combines blue and yellow tiles with no gaps or overlaps; D combines blue and yellow tiles but has a white uncovered region. Ask which one differs by coverage and which differs by color or number of tile types. A text list alone cannot substantiate every geometric property of a drawing; actual student-made patterns and their claimed coverage require visual inspection and teacher scoring.
Visuals.SecondaryLabel: D: uncovered region (not a complete tiling)
Items: C: mixed blue and yellow, complete
D: mixed blue and yellow, uncovered space

Lessons.Title: Finding Area by Decomposing and Rearranging
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Define area precisely, compose and decompose right-triangle and square pieces, and explain equal-area rearrangements.

Area counts equal square units covering a two-dimensional region without gaps or overlap. A drawing with small and large squares cannot be evaluated merely by counting pieces: first express them in a shared unit. If two congruent figures exactly match when overlaid, their areas are equal.

An area-1 square divided diagonally makes two identical triangles, each area 1/2. Reassemble triangles into other non-overlapping figures and justify why their total area is unchanged. The 2017–2019 source also includes tangram-style hands-on construction and student explanations; the digital examples here do not certify that the original manipulatives or full interactive activity have been recreated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Additive area
KeyConcepts.Definition: The area of a union of non-overlapping pieces is the sum of their individual areas.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Decompose into disjoint measurable parts before adding.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 3-by-2 rectangle next to a 1-by-2 rectangle has total area 6 + 2 = 8 square units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Subtract an excluded piece
KeyConcepts.Definition: A target region can be measured as an enclosing region minus one or more holes.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Only subtract regions that are outside the target, and count each once.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 3-by-4 rectangle with a 2-by-2 corner removed has area 12 − 4 = 8 square units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Triangle-square conservation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two congruent half-square triangles together cover one unit square.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Every non-overlapping rearrangement of both unchanged triangles still has area 1 square unit.
KeyConcepts.Example: Four half-square triangle pieces together have total area 4 × 1/2 = 2 square units.

WorkedExamples.Title: Different-sized tiles are not equal square units
WorkedExamples.Question: A region is covered without gaps by two unit squares and four squares whose side length is 1/2 of the unit square. What is its area?
WorkedExamples.Method: Convert each smaller square's area into the same unit-square measure.
Steps: The two unit squares contribute 2 square units.
Each 1/2-by-1/2 square contributes 1/4 of a square unit.
Four small squares contribute 4 × 1/4 = 1 square unit.
The region's total area is 2 + 1 = 3 square units.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 3 square units, not the six counted pieces.
WorkedExamples.Check: If the pieces had gaps or overlaps, the count would not equal the area of the full region.

WorkedExamples.Title: Build the same area from triangles
WorkedExamples.Question: Cut a square of area 1 unit² along a diagonal. What is each triangle's area, and what area do four identical triangles cover after rearranging?
WorkedExamples.Method: Match two triangles to the original square, then use additivity.
Steps: Two congruent triangles exactly recompose the area-1 square.
Each must therefore have area 1/2 square unit.
Four triangles cover 4 × 1/2 = 2 square units.
Moving the four pieces changes the outline but not their combined area.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Each triangle has area 1/2 square unit; four cover 2 square units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Different non-square designs using the four identical pieces are valid if coverage is complete and pieces do not overlap.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two non-square assemblies from four half-square triangles
WorkedExamples.Question: Four congruent right triangles were cut along diagonals of two identical unit squares. Describe two different non-square arrangements using all four triangles without overlap, and justify the area of each.
WorkedExamples.Method: Each unchanged right triangle has area 1/2 square unit; build and describe two distinct connected arrangements with no gaps or overlaps.
Steps: Each original unit square has area 1 square unit and makes two congruent right triangles after cutting along its diagonal.
Each triangle contributes 1/2 square unit, so four such triangles contribute 4 × 1/2 = 2 square units.
Arrange the four pieces as two 1-by-1 squares side by side to make a 2-by-1 non-square rectangle of area 2.
Rearrange the same four unchanged pieces into a connected slanted parallelogram of area 2. A teacher should verify the actual arrangement uses every piece once, without overlap.
Explain that the total remains 2 square units because the four original pieces have not been stretched, discarded or added.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Both valid non-square assemblies cover 2 square units. Their outlines may differ, but each uses exactly four congruent half-square triangles.
WorkedExamples.Check: Require a student sketch, digital manipulation or accessible geometric description; verify each shape is non-square, uses all four pieces and contains no overlaps or gaps.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding areas of pieces that overlap.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The overlapping region is counted twice.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Choose disjoint pieces or subtract the overlap to count every square unit once.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming rearrangement allows stretching a part.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Stretching changes the area and invalidates area conservation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Move and rotate unchanged pieces; use equal square units before and after.

SummaryPoints: Decomposition: add areas of non-overlapping pieces.
Subtraction: enclosing area minus missing pieces.
Rearranging unchanged pieces preserves the total area.

Visuals.Title: Triangle composition and fractional area
Visuals.Description: First-party text-accessible construction: one area-1 unit square is bisected along its diagonal into two congruent right triangles, each with area 1/2 square unit. Rejoin two triangles to make a square or another fitting non-square polygon. Four copies each of area 1/2 cover 2 square units in any non-overlapping assembly.

Lessons.Title: Reasoning to Find Area
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Compare shaded regions and find polygon areas by decomposing, rearranging and subtracting known missing parts.

When a shaded region is moved from one place to another, a missing piece and an exactly matching attached piece can cancel without changing total area. A 4-by-4 shaded square has area 16; removing one unit square and attaching it outside results in 16−1+1=16 square units. The outline changes, but the shaded area does not.

For grid-based figures, combine rectangles or triangles without counting every square. For off-grid figures use labeled perpendicular lengths. If a missing tilted square has unknown area, do not invent its measurement: a valid approach may be to decompose and rearrange surrounding measurable triangles. Explain why each method covers only the shaded part.

KeyConcepts.Title: Decomposition and addition
KeyConcepts.Definition: A region can be partitioned into non-overlapping measurable subregions.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 5-by-4 rectangle excluding a 2-by-2 corner contains 20 − 4 = 16 square units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Enclosing and subtraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: A known enclosing figure gives the area before unwanted parts are removed.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Subtract the area of missing pieces exactly once.
KeyConcepts.Example: From a 6-by-5 rectangle subtract a 3-by-2 missing rectangle to obtain 24 square units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Check equivalent strategies
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two valid methods measuring the same region yield the same area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Match disjoint parts or show the enclosing area minus the complement.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 3-by-8 rectangle covers 24 square units, the same area as a 6-by-5 rectangle with 6 square units removed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Same shaded area with a hole and an attached piece
WorkedExamples.Question: Figure A is a shaded 4-by-4 square. Figure B removes one shaded unit square from A's interior and attaches that same shaded unit square outside. Compare only the shaded regions.
WorkedExamples.Method: Account for the removed and added congruent parts.
Steps: The original square has shaded area 4 × 4 = 16 square units.
Removing a unit square leaves 15 shaded square units.
Reattaching the same piece adds one square unit.
The modified shaded area is 15 + 1 = 16 square units.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The shaded areas are equal; each is 16 square units.
WorkedExamples.Check: The one-square hole is unshaded, while the matching outside attachment is shaded.

WorkedExamples.Title: Enclosing subtraction requires a known hole
WorkedExamples.Question: A 6-by-6 square contains a 3-by-3 unshaded square. How much of the outer region is shaded?
Steps: The outside square covers 6 × 6 = 36 square units.
The unshaded inside square covers 3 × 3 = 9 square units.
Subtract only the hole once: 36−9=27 square units.
WorkedExamples.Check: When the size of an interior tilted hole is unknown, use a justified alternative such as rearranging measured triangles rather than inventing a dimension.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two solutions to a corner-cut region
WorkedExamples.Question: Sketch a shaded nonrectangular region that can be decomposed into measurable triangles and rectangles. Calculate its area in two methods without double-counting.
WorkedExamples.Method: Teacher-reviewed source-aligned proof based on measurable non-overlapping pieces.
Steps: Enclosing area is 5 × 4 = 20; missing corner area is 2 × 2 = 4.
Subtract to get 20 − 4 = 16 square units.
Partition the remaining region into a 5-by-2 strip and a 3-by-2 strip for 10 + 6 = 16.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews region shading, explicit measurements, justification of every part and equality of the two methods.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: This omits part of the shaded region.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Identify the target and remove each unshaded subregion only once.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using a length unit for an area answer.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A rectangular area multiplies two lengths and is measured in square units.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Write square units and show which rectangles or pieces they count.

SummaryPoints: Add non-overlapping areas or subtract missing parts from a known enclosure.
Rearranging equal parts preserves the total area.
Justify with a second method and report square units.

Visuals.Title: Conserved shaded area after moving one square
Visuals.Description: Text-only geometric representation: begin with a 4-by-4 square shaded completely, area 16. In a second figure one unit square is an unshaded interior hole, while a congruent unit square is reattached outside the original boundary. The 15 still-shaded original unit squares plus 1 attached shaded square produce 16 shaded square units. The unshaded interior is not counted.
Items: B: one shaded reattached outside square
SecondaryItems: Shaded area A = shaded area B = 16
